To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
energy optimization in movement kinematics and energy optimization in movement joint angles are independent of each other.

(1) movement kinematics are biased toward energy optimization in goal-directed reaching, (2) energy optimization of joint angles can occur independent of the force exerted by gravity, and (3) energy optimization in joint angles occurs in the same direction as the primary movement kinematics.

the kinematics of goal-directed aiming movements to far targets undershot to a greater extent when moving against gravity compared to moving with the effects of gravity; and the kinematics of aiming movements with rod extensions optimized the contribution of the distal joints to movement end effector displacement.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the brain optimizes the control of movement kinematics and joint angles in order to reduce the energy costs of goal-directed aiming.
the energy optimization in movement kinematics and joint angles.
the role of the central nervous system (CNS) in the planning and control of movement.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

energy optimization in goal-directed reaching is a multi-level phenomenon, with the kinematics of the movement optimizing the movement in consideration of gravity, and the joint angles optimizing the movement independent of gravity.
the energy optimization principle in the control of upper limb movements extends to the control of both joint angles and movement kinematics.
energy optimization in goal-directed reaching movements is not restricted to movement kinematics but is also evident in joint angle kinematics.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
energy optimization in movement kinematics and joint angles are both involved in the control of upper limb movements in goal-directed aiming.

the control of joint angle trajectories in goal-directed aiming movements is organized to minimize the amount of energy required to move the limb in consideration of the direction and magnitude of the force of gravitational acceleration.
energy optimization occurs in both movement kinematics and joint angles, and that these two components of movement control are coordinated to optimize energy expenditure in goal-directed aiming.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the control of movement kinematics is not independent of the control of movement dynamics.
the optimization of joint angles in goal-directed aiming is not limited to the shoulder joint, as previously thought, but extends to the elbow joint as well.
the optimization of energy expenditure in goal-directed aiming extends to the control of joint angle kinematics, which is a critical component of the two-component models of movement.
